description: We are a multidisciplinary team blending software development, data visualization, and aerospace engineering. For the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge, we're building an integrated map using NASA Mars mission data to support astronaut Marswalk planning, paired with a fixed-wing UAV concept engineered for Mars' thin atmosphere and low gravity as a future exploration data source.
summary: MARTIAN MAP is a UAV-supported mapping and route planning system that helps astronauts plan and carry out safe, efficient Marswalks. A VTOL (vertical takeoff and landing) fixed-wing UAV flies ahead of the crew and scans a 6–7 km corridor in the Jezero Crater region. Its cameras and LiDAR collect fine-scale terrain data that orbital imagery cannot resolve, such as rock fields, micro-ridges and dust pockets. We fuse this with NASA orbital datasets (HiRISE, CTX, THEMIS and CRISM) into a layered, updated hazard map. The system classifies terrain into low, medium and high-risk zones and recommends routes that balance slope, roughness, dust risk and data confidence, not just distance. Results appear on the astronaut's helmet display, wrist display and a Mission Control Dashboard, and routes are recomputed when new obstacles appear. Our design is based on analytical calculations, and the interface prototype runs on simulated terrain data. Hardware testing is planned.
details:
What it does and how it works

Martian Map is a layered, integrated view of a Mars surface route that helps an astronaut plan and carry out a safe Marswalk. Orbital data cannot show small rock fields, sharp ridges or loose dust along a walking route, so we add local scouting. A VTOL (vertical takeoff and landing) fixed-wing UAV flies ahead of the crew along the route and observes the terrain. The system combines these observations with NASA orbital data (HiRISE and CTX imagery, THEMIS thermal data, CRISM mineral data and a CTX-based elevation model of Jezero Crater) in a single map. Terrain is classified as low, medium or high risk, and the recommended route is updated when a new hazard appears. Mission control sees the full detail, while the astronaut sees only critical information on a wrist display and helmet HUD.

Benefits

The crew gets a current, local view of the terrain ahead of them. This helps them avoid hazards, save time and reduce risk during an EVA.

Intended impact

We aim to make future crewed Marswalks safer and faster to plan, leaving more time for science along the route.

Tools and technologies

We used NASA Mars Trek, USGS CTX elevation data and NASA HiRISE imagery for the terrain layers. We designed the UAV in SolidWorks and built a web simulation and interface to demonstrate the mission. We used ChatGPT and Claude as AI tools to support our work on the project.

What is creative

We combine NASA's orbital maps with an aerial scout designed for Mars's thin atmosphere. Our route logic weighs risk, not only distance, and each user sees only the level of detail they need.

Factors we considered

We considered Mars's thin atmosphere (about 0.020 kg/m³), low Reynolds number, extreme cold, dust on solar cells, energy limits and vehicle mass. We also state our limits clearly: performance values are calculation-based, obstacles in the interface are simulated, and our current mass estimate (8.78 kg) is above the 6.0 kg target. Hardware testing is the next step.
